paras: The Tackett's Mills riot was a fight between white and Black men at a country store at Tackett's Mills, Stafford County, Virginia, on Christmas Day 1888. A white man, Bennett (or Benton) Heflin, was shot dead, and a Black man, named Henry Brown in a later report, died of his injuries. Papers across the country reported it as a 'race riot' arising from the recent election, and Fredericksburg feared further trouble.

Tackett's Mills lay about twenty miles from Fredericksburg, in a part of Stafford County where, according to the wire report, whites were the majority and mostly Democrats. The county itself had lately been giving large Republican majorities, the Richmond Daily Times noted. White and Black men gathered at a store kept by L. A. Skinner, which the Richmond Dispatch called L. K. Skinner's, to spend Christmas.

The talk turned to the election, with all of the Black men and a few whites arguing that Stafford was Republican and the other whites holding it for the Democrats. In the first reports, Heflin and an unnamed Black man carried the argument into a personal quarrel over a plow and came to blows, and a general fight followed with guns, sticks and rocks. Heflin fell dead from a bullet through the heart, which the Daily Times said was 'supposed' to have been fired by the man he had quarreled with.

According to the Daily Times, the whites then 'turned with great fury upon the negroes,' and many on both sides were seriously hurt. The Black man who had fought Heflin tried to escape but was captured and died of his injuries, according to the Times and the Alexandria Gazette; the wire said he lived only several minutes. A second wire version put the number dangerously injured at twenty.

A Dispatch correspondent's later account from Fredericksburg named the participants as three Heflin brothers, Warren, Benton and Thomas, and two Black men, Henry Brown and George Black, and traced the fight to an old grudge as well as politics. In this version Benton Heflin knocked Brown down and began beating him on the floor, and in the general fight that followed George Black shot Heflin through the heart. Black escaped, was pursued and was reported jailed, while Brown later died of his injuries.

The sheriff and a posse went to the scene and arrested several men said to have taken part. W. S. White, the Commonwealth's attorney for the county, left Fredericksburg to investigate, and the Dispatch reported that all parties connected with the affair were being arrested. Heflin was married and left a wife and two children. No report of an inquest, indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

The story reached the press as a Fredericksburg dispatch on December 27, which the New York Evening World ran under 'More Race Riots' beside news of a Mississippi outbreak. Wilmington and Waterbury papers carried a shortened form as 'Race Fight in Virginia' on December 28. A second version, sent by way of Chicago, called it a 'bloody battle' on Christmas eve and ran in Indianapolis, Wheeling, Sacramento, Abbeville and Louisville through December 31, sometimes grouped with other Christmas race clashes.

Headlines stressed the color line: 'White Against Black' in Wheeling and 'The War in the South' in Sacramento, which placed the town in West Virginia. The Richmond Daily Times headed its special 'RACE RIOT' and 'The Serene State of Stafford Sorely Shaken up,' lamenting a 'dark spot' on the county's peaceful name without assigning blame. Only the Richmond Dispatch named the Black men, and its account had a white man strike the first blow.

The accounts differ on the date, with most giving Christmas Day, the Chicago version Christmas eve and the Dispatch 'last Wednesday,' which would be December 26. They also differ on who struck first and who died: the early reports merged Heflin's attacker and the Black man who died, whereas the Dispatch, the later and more detailed local report, said Heflin beat Brown first and that a different man, George Black, did the shooting.

reader.title: Tackett's Mills riot
bases: A quarrel at a store grew into a general fight between white and Black men in which a white man was shot dead and, by the local account, the whites then 'turned with great fury upon the negroes' and a Black man died of his injuries (A1, A5, A8).

Two wire versions (A1, A9) and two Richmond reports (A5, A8) agree that a white man named Heflin was shot dead and a Black man died after a political quarrel at Tackett's Mills, though they differ on names, date and sequence.

accounts.gist: A Christmas-afternoon election argument led Hiflen and an unnamed Black man into a personal quarrel over a plough; in the general riot Hiflen was shot dead and the Black man, 'badly mutilated', lived several minutes.

accounts.label: Richmond Daily Times special
accounts.gist: Heflin was shot, 'supposed' by the Black man he quarreled with; the whites then turned on the Black men, and the man who attacked Heflin tried to flee, was captured and later died of his injuries.

accounts.label: Second wire version (via Chicago)
accounts.gist: A 'bloody battle' on Christmas eve: Hiflen was shot dead, his 'colored enemy' was also shot and lived several minutes, and twenty were dangerously injured.

accounts.label: Richmond Dispatch correspondent
accounts.gist: The fight began between the three Heflin brothers and Henry Brown and George Black over an old grudge and politics; Benton Heflin knocked Brown down and beat him, Black shot Heflin dead and fled, and Brown later died.

framing.detail: The Richmond Daily Times ran 'RACE RIOT' and 'The Serene State of Stafford Sorely Shaken up', describing a 'dark spot' on the 'peaceful old State of Stafford' and blaming no side outright while calling Heflin's shooting 'the bloody deed'.
Northern and western papers ran the wire as 'More Race Riots', 'Race Fight in Virginia', 'White Against Black' and 'The War in the South', often beside other Christmas race clashes.
The Richmond Dispatch's follow-up named the Black men, reported that Benton Heflin knocked Brown down and began beating him, and recorded Heflin's family.
